result:
The smallest guaranteed count is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor\binom{q}{2}$. This is the number of bowties in $K^q_{\lceil n/2\rceil,\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ itself. I did not verify from the literature that no graph with spectral radius at least $\lambda(K^q)$ has fewer bowties, so that part rests on the assumption that the extremal graph is the one given.

**Triangles in $K^q$.** Let $A$ (size $\lceil n/2\rceil$) carry the $q$ disjoint edges $e_1,\dots,e_q$, and let $B$ (size $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$) be independent. A triangle needs an edge inside $A$, since $B$ is independent and the graph is otherwise bipartite. Two inside-$A$ edges cannot lie in one triangle because the $e_i$ are disjoint. So every triangle is $e_i \cup \{w\}$ with $w\in B$, giving $q\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ triangles.

**Bowties.** Two triangles $e_i\cup\{w\}$ and $e_j\cup\{w'\}$ share exactly one vertex only in one way:
- If $w = w'$, the triangles share only $w$ when $i\ne j$, since $e_i$ and $e_j$ are disjoint. This gives $\lfloor n/2\rfloor\binom{q}{2}$ bowties.
- If $w\ne w'$, the only possible shared vertex would lie in $A$, which forces $i=j$ and shares two vertices. No bowties arise here.

Hence $K^q_{\lceil n/2\rceil,\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ contains $\lfloor n/2\rfloor\binom{q}{2}$ bowties.

ANSWER: $\lfloor n/2\rfloor\binom{q}{2}$
